name: PIQA: Physical Interaction Question Answering
description: A benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. The dataset consists of multiple choice questions where models must choose the most sensible solution to achieve a physical goal, testing knowledge of everyday objects, their properties, affordances, and how they can be manipulated.

creator.name: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
creator.affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Microsoft Research AI, Carnegie Mellon University, Paul G. Allen School for Computer Science and Engineering, University of Washington

publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
citeAs: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi. PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI 2020.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected through crowdsourced annotation using instructables.com as inspiration. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables from six categories (costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop) to encourage thinking about atypical solutions and non-prototypical uses of everyday objects. Annotators provided goal-solution pairs where they articulated a physical goal and both a valid solution and an invalid trick solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source was instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for various tasks from cooking to car repair. Users on instructables provide images or videos detailing each step and lists of required tools. Annotators were asked to glance at instructables and pull out or be inspired to construct two component tasks.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Examples with low agreement during validation were removed from the data, particularly those requiring expert level domain knowledge that should not fall under commonsense. The AFLite algorithm was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples from the data. AFLite performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. 5,000 examples were used to fine-tune BERT-Large and compute embeddings of remaining instances. An ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets determined whether pre-computed embeddings were strong indicators of correct answers. All text was tokenized by Spacy and examples were truncated at 150 tokens (affecting 1% of data).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were asked to provide: 1) a physical goal (often centered on atypical materials), 2) a valid solution to achieve it, and 3) a trick/permutation that makes the solution invalid, often subtly due to misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. Two examples were drawn per instructable to encourage one to come later in the process and require precise articulation of pre-conditions. The interface included a diff button which highlighted where solutions differ, improving annotator accuracy and speed. Annotators were qualified through a qualification HIT containing well-constructed and underspecified goal-solution pairs, requiring >80% success rate to participate.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed. Annotators used both simple linguistic tricks (e.g., negation and numerical changes) and often swapped a key action or item for another that was topically similar but not helpful. The two solutions may differ by as little as one word. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple annotations per item during validation phase for agreement checking
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm for artifact removal, BERT-Large for computing embeddings during bias reduction, Spacy for tokenization
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was specifically designed to remove annotation artifacts using the AFLite algorithm to address stylistic artifacts and trivial examples that have been shown to artificially inflate model performance on previous NLI benchmarks. The algorithm discards instances whose feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. Despite these efforts, reporting bias remains a challenge as prototypical solutions and common objects (e.g., kitchen tools) were initially overrepresented before using instructables as prompts to flatten the distribution of referenced objects.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on physical commonsense that can be expressed in language, but due to reporting bias, many commonsense properties are rarely directly reported. The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Some correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g., special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under commonsense. Manual inspection of development errors showed that some 'mistakes' are actually correct but required a web search to verify. Future research may match humans on the dataset by finding large sources of in-domain data and fine-tuning heavily, but this misses the philosophical point that knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for: 1) Training and evaluating natural language understanding models on physical commonsense reasoning, 2) Testing the ability of models to link text to intuitive physics models of the world, 3) Diagnostic evaluation to probe the inner workings of deep pretrained language models and determine the extent of their physical knowledge, 4) Benchmarking progress towards language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced. The dataset includes 16,000+ training QA pairs with 2K development and 3K test splits. Not recommended for: claiming human-level physical understanding without actual world interaction.
